title: UK cyber shortfalls: A skills gap and/or a gender gap?
raw_text:
Code First Girls has teamed up with a host of public and private players to address a dual gap currently putting the UK on the backfoot when it comes to cyber security.

It’s estimated that the country is facing a three million tech worker shortfall over the next decade. This is an issue that derives, at first glance, from a skills gap that the industry has sleepwalked into thanks to seeing cyber security as a technical function rather than a business-critical capability.

Intertwining with this structural misstep, however, is a very noticeable gap in who is being attracted and encouraged into the cyber workforce in the first place – a gender gap.

“The most concerning trend is the scale of the skills gap combined with the under-representation of women in the sector. The UK needs millions more tech workers, yet women still make up a small proportion of the workforce, meaning a huge portion of talent is being underutilised,” says Anna Brailsford, CEO and co-founder of Code First Girls.

“Organisations continue to rely on a narrow pool of talent with similar backgrounds, which can actually lead to blind spots in how risks are identified and managed. Cyber security requires not just technical expertise, but problem-solving, adaptability and an understanding of human behaviour.”

A lack of diversity naturally and immediately shrinks the ability to unlock those diverse skillsets and perspectives. The mission at Code First Girls is therefore to open the minds of both employers and prospective employees who might not have considered entering the tech space before.

“More than just enter it, but to progress and lead within it,” Brailsford adds.

Pathway visibility

Over the years, Code First Girls has provided more than 300,000 free learning opportunities for women. The gauge of success, however, runs deeper than just exposure and initial training.

“What defines us is outcomes – getting people into real jobs and helping businesses access job-ready, diverse talent at scale,” says Brailsford. “We work at the intersection of the digital skills gap and the gender gap, partnering directly with employers to place and accelerate women in cyber roles at scale.

“One of the biggest issues is visibility of pathways. If you don’t see how you get into the industry, or don’t see people like you in it, it’s much harder to imagine yourself there. That’s something we’ve worked hard to change by making pathways into tech much more visible and accessible.”

Tech and cyber security has been positioned, often unintentionally, as a male-dominated field, blocking a clear line of sight for women who didn’t earmark the industry through their education routes and initial career choices. One of Code First Girls’ chief missions, to that end, is to alter the mindset of what constitutes a suitable candidate in a cyber role.

Brailsford says: “Rigid education routes have made it harder for career switchers or people from non-traditional backgrounds to enter the sector. At the same time, workplace cultures and structures haven’t always supported retention and progression, which has contributed to the drop-off we see.

“Technical skills are important, but they’re only part of the picture. Cyber security also requires critical thinking, problem-solving, communication and the ability to work under pressure. Understanding risk, being able to analyse patterns and thinking creatively about potential threats are all key. Many of these are highly transferable skills, which is why career switchers can be incredibly successful in the field,” she says.

Reach and teach

But where to find people who might consider a switch of career? And how do you convince them that their skillsets and capabilities might suit a role in cyber security?

Events such as the Cyber Security Skills Summit have been driven by Code First Girls to tick the exposure box. They dovetail seamlessly with training programmes and outreach initiatives designed to fulfil reach and teach objectives. This includes the creation of a cyber security and vulnerability research (VR) training programme in collaboration with the UK’s leading national security agency.

“Partnerships are central to what we do. We work closely with employers to ensure our training aligns with real-world needs, and to create direct pathways into roles,” Brailsford adds. “We also collaborate with government and industry bodies to scale impact. Being part of the [erstwhile] DSIT’s Women in Tech taskforce led by Liz Kendall is a significant milestone, as is the strong partnership we’ve developed with Lloyds Banking Group.”

The latter partnership involves Code First Girls providing structured pathways for women to move into tech careers, and Lloyds offering a direct route into engineering, data and cyber security roles within the organisation. Lloyds Banking Group (LBG) sponsors places on Code First Girls Degrees with the chance to then join their Data & AI or Tech Engineering graduate schemes.

“For me, it fits clearly into our broader approach to early careers,” says Richard Horvath, lead software engineer within the Transport Platform at LBG. “Whether it’s CFG’s programmes, bootcamps or sponsored degrees, individuals are getting real technical capability and, just as importantly, the confidence to step into a tech role.”

LBG’s role is to then further support growth in a more practical environment. “On a personal level, it’s been so rewarding to give more women a fair opportunity to demonstrate their potential, while also maintaining strong engineering standards,” says Horvath. “We need that diversity in our workforce if we’re going to drive innovation, because different perspectives lead to better ideas, better problem solving and ultimately better outcomes.”

He notes the tangible impact that this partnership is having not just on industry gaps, but people’s lives: “Having been involved in early careers for over five years, I’ve seen how powerful these opportunities can be and CFG is one of the strongest examples of that in action.”

A different starting point

Clarissa Sorger is a behavioural scientist at LBG’s AI Centre of Excellence, Chief Data & AI Office. She knows first-hand how critical opportunities for exposure and growth are to encourage career progression having been selected for ‘Elevate’, a leadership and career advancement programme for women in tech at LBG.

Sorger knows what such opportunities offered at scale could do for those who hadn’t even considered cyber as a prospect until now. “I believe such initiatives make you feel appreciated and invested in, and boost your confidence,” she says. “For me, it’s made it all the more inspiring to see graduates leverage their expertise from the Code First Programme to thrive in LBG’s fast-paced and ever-changing environment, despite often not coming from a traditional coding background.

“It’s the perfect illustration of where your drive, curiosity and commitment can take you in a short space of time, even if you start out from a different point than some of your [male] peers.”

Short-term sacrifice for long-term opportunity

Vicki Gibbison is a software engineer currently 19 months into her graduate programme at LBG, and is a prime example of someone who’s taken the “long way around” to reach a cyber destination.

From experience as a lifeguard, fitness instructor, NVQ assessor, mother of two, nail technician, beauty therapist and psychology graduate – in that order – Code First Girls quenched a developing thirst for a dabble in tech.

“CFG gave me the opportunity to deepen and strengthen my technical skills in a supportive, inclusive environment, surrounded by people who were learning from a similar starting point,” Gibbison says. “And that supportive culture has continued since joining Lloyds Banking Group.

“Coming into a large organisation as a career‑switcher, I was worried I might be judged or seen as less capable because I didn’t follow a traditional technical route. Instead, my line manager and team created an environment where questions were welcomed and learning was actively encouraged.”

Technically, the learning curve has been steep, Gibbison trained in everything from building databases and writing complex queries, to developing full‑stack applications, understanding system architecture, working with agile methodologies and contributing to real projects. She’s now eager to pursue a development path towards ultimately becoming a senior engineer.

“Programmes like Code First Girls are intense, especially for women balancing work, families and other commitments, but it’s important to remember that choosing to change career often means short‑term sacrifice for long‑term opportunity,” she adds. “You become motivated by the realisation that there is space for women in tech. Not just to enter, but to thrive, lead and help shape the future of the industry.”

Leading, not just participating

The phrase “shaping the future” is a common rallying cry both from both those who have entered the industry through this route and those providing the route.

Sharon Doherty, chief people and places officer at LBG, notes: “Through our partnership with Code First Girls, we are helping more women build practical technical skills and move into roles where they can apply them, strengthening our teams and supporting a more inclusive pipeline of next gen talent.”

A wave of positive momentum at this scale is still novel when it comes to addressing both the skills and gender gap from a cyber security perspective. “While we are seeing progress, we’re not yet where we need to be,” Horvath confirms.

But there is plenty of reason for optimism courtesy of Code First Girls which now sits in the middle of an ever-expanding network pushing towards the same goal.

Brailsford picks up the thread: “That optimism comes from a growing recognition among both government and industry that the skills gap and diversity gap need to be addressed together. We’re seeing more collaboration, more investment and more openness to alternative pathways into tech and cyber security.

“We are on a better trajectory, but we’re not moving fast enough yet. To really close the gap, we need to scale what works, which is flexible training models, employer-led pathways, and a stronger focus on retention and progression, not just entry. If we can do that, there’s a real opportunity to unlock a much broader talent pool,” she says.

Sorger adds: “I hope more women with an interest in data and tech feel empowered to sign up to initiatives such as Code First Girls. In a very short space of time, they can obtain an accreditation and secure a space to join a grad scheme with a top employer. I believe this goes to show how quickly life can change if you take opportunities – especially the daunting ones.”

As the momentum builds, the hope is that individual success stories being seen today will evolve into systemic nationwide change so that uptake can outpace the drop off.

Brailsford concludes: “For Code First Girls, that means continuing to scale our impact and reach more individuals and employers. More broadly, it means building a cyber workforce that is more inclusive, more diverse and better equipped to meet the demands of the future economy.

“Ultimately, success would be a sector where access to tech and cyber security careers is determined by potential, not background, and where women are not just participating, but leading.”

Code First Girls has teamed up with a host of public and private players to address a dual gap currently putting the UK on the backfoot when it comes to cyber security.

It’s estimated that the country is facing a three million tech worker shortfall over the next decade. This is an issue that derives, at first glance, from a skills gap that the industry has sleepwalked into thanks to seeing cyber security as a technical function rather than a business-critical capability.

Intertwining with this structural misstep, however, is a very noticeable gap in who is being attracted and encouraged into the cyber workforce in the first place – a gender gap.

“The most concerning trend is the scale of the skills gap combined with the under-representation of women in the sector. The UK needs millions more tech workers, yet women still make up a small proportion of the workforce, meaning a huge portion of talent is being underutilised,” says Anna Brailsford, CEO and co-founder of Code First Girls.

“Organisations continue to rely on a narrow pool of talent with similar backgrounds, which can actually lead to blind spots in how risks are identified and managed. Cyber security requires not just technical expertise, but problem-solving, adaptability and an understanding of human behaviour.”

A lack of diversity naturally and immediately shrinks the ability to unlock those diverse skillsets and perspectives.

title: Gartner: Why the cloud is holding back agentic AI
raw_text:
Agentic operations are rapidly transitioning from experimental tools to active participants in enterprise workflows. Unlike traditional generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) applications that primarily produce content, agentic systems interact with tools – namely application programming interfaces (APIs), retrieve corporate information and execute changes in enterprise systems – opening unprecedented opportunities for automation.  

This evolution from passive content generation to active and autonomous participation marks a fundamental shift in the role of AI in the enterprise. 

However, as organisations race to deploy these advanced technologies, they face a foundational barrier: the cloud architecture that powered the past decade of digital transformations is now holding back the agentic AI revolution, mainly for real-time and agentic AI use cases. Legacy, cloud-centric datacentres, built for batch processing and human-in-the-loop workflows, cannot support the continuous, high-frequency inference these advanced AI-driven systems demand. 

To deliver autonomous AI at scale, infrastructure and operations leaders need to address the latency, bandwidth costs and outage risks inherent to centralised cloud networks. As a result, hybrid edge-cloud architecture emerges as a strategic imperative – an architectural shift that delivers the resilience, cost-efficiency and autonomy required to scale AI initiatives rapidly and securely. 

The latency barrier 

Here’s the uncomfortable bit: for agentic and real-time AI to work in the way suppliers are promising, infrastructure and operations leaders need sub-millisecond response times. Cloud-only architecture makes it difficult to deliver the same every time. The round trip from a device to a distant datacentre and back is too long when milliseconds are the difference between an outcome and a near-miss. 

Think about what’s being asked of these systems: robotic control on a factory floor, predictive maintenance on industrial kit that’s about to fail, fraud detection that needs to catch a transaction before it clears. All these need decision loops under 10 milliseconds. That’s not a nice-to-have benchmark – it’s the physics of the problem. The further data has to travel, the longer it takes and the more it costs, and no amount of clever engineering changes that basic constraint. 

This is exactly why edge computing has stopped being a niche networking conversation and started showing up in board-level infrastructure discussions. It’s not a trend chasing hype – it’s a response to real deployments hitting a real wall. For safety-critical use cases in manufacturing, healthcare and industrial automation, that latency isn’t an annoyance – it’s a risk nobody wants to own. And the research backs this up, with this shift now looking critical for nearly every agentic AI use case that’s both latency-sensitive and high bandwidth.  

Organisations still betting everything on centralised cloud are more exposed to outages and watching their costs climb at the same time, which is a rough combination when the board is asking why the AI programme isn’t scaling faster. 

Overcoming unsustainable bandwidth costs 

Then there’s the cost. Beyond the challenge of latency, centralised processing creates a significant economic hurdle: unsustainable bandwidth and data egress costs. Real-time AI applications, especially those involving video and voice analytics or high-frequency sensor inputs, generate a torrent of data. Transmitting these massive, continuous streams to a central cloud for processing is economically unviable at scale. 

Hyperscaler egress fees, which average between $0.05 and $0.09 per gigabyte, can quickly spiral. Gartner estimates suggest that these fees alone can constitute 10% to 15% of total cloud spending for data-heavy workloads. Consider a deployment of 1,000 high-definition cameras operating at 5Mbps – this annually generates approximately 54PB (petabytes) of data, incurring an estimated $4.6m per year in egress costs alone. 

This is where edge computing becomes an economic game-changer. By locally processing data, organisations can filter raw streams and transmit only relevant metadata or critical events to the cloud. This approach can reduce upstream data volumes by 60% to 90%. In the camera example, edge filtering could slash the annual egress cost to $1.38m, yielding a saving of more than $3.2m.  

By shifting AI workloads to edge environments, organisations can achieve up to an 85% reduction in overall bandwidth and operational costs compared with cloud-only approaches, transforming the financial viability of large-scale AI deployments.

  • Can edge computing make AI more sustainable? AI’s power demands and associated environmental impact are significant. Edge computing can alleviate some strain, but it’s not a universal solution and doesn't suit all workloads.

A new architectural model

To overcome these limitations, leading organisations are adopting hybrid edge-cloud architectures that process data closer to its source. This model does not replace the cloud – it redefines its role. In this split architectural approach, the edge and the cloud perform the tasks for which they are best suited. 

The edge handles the immediate, real-time workloads – perception, data filtering and initial decision-making. This is where the sub-10-millisecond inference happens, enabling the system to act instantly. The cloud, freed from processing every raw data point, is reserved for less time-sensitive, computationally intensive tasks such as long-term reasoning, coordination, global policy management and the retraining of AI models. This hybrid model delivers the best of both worlds – the low-latency responsiveness and resilience of the edge, combined with the massive scale and analytical power of the cloud. 

Beyond pure cost efficiency, this decentralised model enhances digital sovereignty and data privacy by keeping sensitive information in a local environment, thereby reducing regulatory and geopolitical exposure. 

A playbook for the agentic AI edge 

For IT infrastructure and operations leaders, the path forward requires a structured approach to modernisation. The first step is to audit legacy infrastructure to identify latency-sensitive workloads – such as real-time analytics, instant decision engines and voice and video AI – that can no longer tolerate the delays of cloud-only processing. These become the priority candidates for migration to edge-enabled platforms equipped with AI accelerators. 

Second, organisations must adopt an edge-first mandate for these critical applications, redesigning cost and operating models around decentralised data preprocessing. This involves running pilot projects to quantify the reductions in transmission costs and latency before expanding proven models across the enterprise. 

Finally, this strategy must be underpinned by integrated governance across a distributed environment, creating aligned IT and operations technology operating models with standardised security and observability. Gartner estimates that by 2029, 50% of enterprises will be using edge computing (up from 20% in 2024), so delaying this strategy is no longer a viable option. The market is increasingly shifting towards edge-first, hybrid AI as the new standard for enterprise innovation. Organisations that fail to modernise for AI are not just at risk – they are on a path to AI irrelevance.

Pankil Sheth is an associate principal analyst at Gartner, specialising in unified communications and collaboration infrastructure and applications.

title: CW@60: The moment technology became personal
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

I grew up in Glasgow and studied at Strathclyde. I didn’t set out with a fixed plan to build a career in technology, but I was always drawn to it. One chapter stands out. I found myself in Silicon Valley, living and working through the dot com boom, and it shaped how I’ve thought about technology ever since.

It was an extraordinary place to be at that time. Ideas were becoming companies almost overnight, established ways of working were being torn up and rebuilt, and there was a real sense of possibility in the air - exhilarating and unsettling in equal measure.

It was an education you couldn’t get anywhere else - a front-row seat as an entire industry decided, in real time, what the future was going to look like.

What stayed with me wasn’t the hype. It was watching how people responded to that much change and uncertainty. Some hesitated, some leaned in, and confidence was often what separated them. I’ve carried that experience with me through the rest of my career, from implementing systems for clients and working at the intersection of technology and risk to leading PwC UK’s technology and innovation agenda.

Technology, opportunity and trust

At its best, technology creates new opportunities for growth and innovation, opening doors that simply weren’t there before and giving people the means to pursue them. Every development also brings new risks to navigate. The organisations that get furthest are the ones that treat managing those risks as a way to build trust and enable progress, not as something that slows it down.

The risk side of my career brought that into focus - understanding uncertainty, managing exposure, and helping organisations govern the complexity that new technology brings while still driving value from it. Those that did it best didn’t use risk as a reason to stand still - they used it to earn the trust to move forward.

That matters because technology is about far more than systems and infrastructure. It changes how decisions get made, helping people weigh uncertainty, challenge assumptions and make better calls. The value is not only in making processes smoother or tasks quicker, but in helping people deliver better outcomes and stand behind the decisions that led to them. Judgement isn’t replaced - it’s sharpened.

Leading through the AI shift

We’re living through another one of those moments now, and I don’t say that lightly. What’s happening with AI is bigger. The capital flowing into it, the speed at which it is moving, and its reach across every sector are on a scale I never saw in Silicon Valley. Unlike then, this change isn’t confined to one place - it is reshaping how work is done everywhere, all at once.

“Looking ahead, I think we talk too much about what technology can do, and not nearly enough about what people and organisations need from it”

Claire Reid

AI is driving an unprecedented pace of change for employees and organisations alike, bringing real opportunity alongside real uncertainty. What strikes me most is how quickly things now move from pilot or proof of concept into full deployment. What once took years is happening in months.

That is why AI is no longer simply a technology issue - it is a leadership issue. People are asking what it means for their role, their skills and what comes next. The organisations that succeed will be the ones that help their people make sense of the change and benefit from it, not simply those that deploy the tools fastest.

What I find genuinely interesting is what organisations are now hiring for. Our AI Jobs Barometer, drawn from more than a billion job ads worldwide, found that roles where AI takes on the routine work are growing twice as fast as those where it doesn’t, and that they increasingly call for judgement, creativity and leadership.

As AI absorbs more of the routine, the questions that matter most are the ones it can’t settle on its own - is this the right call, can we stand behind it, what do we do next?

In conversations with clients, I see leaders grappling with this every day. Our latest UK CEO Survey found nearly six in 10 UK CEOs are personally sponsoring transformation programmes, while 61% say they face increased scrutiny on their leadership decisions.

Leaders aren’t only implementing new technology - they are being asked to bring their people with them.

Looking forward and realising potential

Looking ahead, I think we talk too much about what technology can do, and not nearly enough about what people and organisations need from it. It’s easy to get swept up in conversations about new platforms and capabilities, but at the core of any transformation are the people using those tools, backed by the skills, support and trust they need to use them well.

That also means recognising that no organisation can realise the potential of technology alone. The pace and complexity of change make strong technology alliances increasingly important, bringing together the best technology, expertise and ideas.

For me, the opportunity is in combining those ecosystems with deep sector expertise, human judgement and trusted relationships to create outcomes that genuinely matter.

I feel genuinely optimistic. Not because anyone can predict exactly where these technologies are headed, but because I’ve spent a career watching people rise to meet the change in front of them.

For leaders, that means holding two things at once - keep moving forward with the technology but invest just as much in helping people use it well. Be honest about the risks and clear about how you’re managing them.

In my experience, that is what earns the trust to move quickly, not what holds you back.

Claire Reid is chief technology & innovation officer at PwC UK.

title: CW@60: This computer malarkey - one life-changing moment after another
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

"I think there might be something in this computer malarkey," my mother said, as we approached my GCSE choices.

Looking back, it was clearly a conversation my parents had after my school parents' evening, when Mum heard about the GCSE options on offer. Information technology GCSE was the new kid on the block and the first of its kind at my school. Its announcement received a mixed reception and I would love to have heard the conversation that followed when Mum and Dad got home.

I was deep in my teenage years, convinced I was pulling off a black wardrobe complete with gothic scarves while declaring my love for Guns N’ Roses and Metallica. Yet somehow, between them, my parents gently nudged me towards a future none of us could really see. A life shaped by this thing called computing.

Micro moments

What stays with me most are the micro moments.

One was the time we upgraded our BBC computer. Dad and I assembled what felt like a piece of technology from the future. He had bought me a couple of games, The 7th Guest and Day of the Tentacle. They made such an impression, I still have the boxes and discs carefully stored away today.

Going from a green screen to computer graphics felt nothing short of magical. We could hardly believe what we were seeing, then the music boomed out of these new speakers as if we had stepped into a live concert. Our faces lit up with a mixture of excitement and disbelief. I was jumping up and down while Dad, naturally, remained just a little more composed. We hurried off to fetch Mum so she could see this impossibly advanced machine.

The micro moments kept coming. Learning Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V at work was a revelation. A colleague shared their newfound expertise and suddenly the world seemed to change in an instant. We genuinely paused at our desks to marvel at what this simple shortcut could do. It sounds ridiculous now but at the time we kept giggling for days, our lives had just become that little bit simpler.

“Technology may change our world but its secret power is its ability to bring people together. Whether those moments leave us feeling amazed, confused, excited, challenged or occasionally completely baffled, the connections and memories they create are bigger than the technology itself”

Avril Chester

Years later came a very different kind of moment. Less revelation, more confusion. Suddenly everyone seemed to be talking in hashtags. What on earth was this # symbol doing in conversations? And why was I the only one who seemed not to get it? Tentatively, I posted my first tweet and first LinkedIn update, convinced I was about to break some unwritten rule of the internet. Nothing happened. Nobody cared. Yet I still checked obsessively for hours afterwards.

Technology evokes emotion. One moment it makes you feel brilliantly clever, the next completely out of your depth.

Life changing

At 37, I experienced a life-changing event. The kind that rips up the tracks beneath you with no obvious route forward. As I slowly began to emerge, beyond the support of immediate family and friends, a number of other voices started offering advice. Take it easy now. Let go of your ambitions. Walk away from your career and do something else.

It wasn't just one voice. If I'm honest, I started to believe them. Then through social media, I met someone further along a remarkably similar journey. He had experienced even greater disruption and was thriving in his career. We connected, he became a mentor and he gave me perhaps the most valuable advice of my professional life, “Don't listen. Do your thing”.

With renewed confidence that I could still have a career, I dusted myself off and started attending conferences again, learning how technology had evolved and building new connections. I'd been away for a year but I knew I still had something to contribute. I waved goodbye to my parents once more after returning home to rebuild - with more scarves, this time in brighter colours - determined not to become a cliché who found purpose in adversity. Naturally, that's exactly what happened.

From one inspirational connection on social media, I forged ahead, eventually becoming a founder and chief technology officer. Imagine that - squeaky, high-pitched-voice me, learning to encourage teams, lead departments and occasionally put out fires (literally, in a datacentre).

What fascinates me isn't the technology itself but what it can achieve. How can we use it to improve lives? Connect people to the information and services they need? Design with the whole of society in mind and avoid leaving people behind?

Some of my best memories are the workshops and hackathons (or heffalumps as Mum calls them). A room full of inspired talent driving towards a common goal, exploring different routes and possibilities together, occasionally grabbing a piece of now very cold pizza because we were too busy creating to stop. The best bits are us.

Secret powers

Technology may change our world but its secret power is its ability to bring people together. Whether those moments leave us feeling amazed, confused, excited, challenged or occasionally completely baffled, the connections and memories they create are bigger than the technology itself.

That's why I struggle to choose one defining moment, I feel incredibly fortunate to have so many.

As we learn to navigate a new world, Computer Weekly has once again hit on the most important story as it celebrates its 60th anniversary. While technology provides the backdrop, it's the people, conversations and shared experiences around it that bring it to life.

It'll be fascinating to see what memories are made next in an AI world. My parents were right - shh, don't tell them that. There really is something in this computer malarkey.

Avril Chester is chief operating officer at AI venture studio Ainad, co-founder of The Human Intelligence Circle, lead author of Leading with humanity in an AI world, founder of Cancer Central, and former CTO at the Royal Pharmaceutical Society.
